notes.meaning: God spoke to Moses just before Israel entered Canaan, reminding the new generation to bring Him their offerings on schedule. Calling the sacrifices My food showed that worship belongs completely to God and must be done as He commands. These regular gifts of animals, grain, and wine symbolized fellowship and peace between the Lord and His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest this sacrificial calendar was compiled by a later editor from earlier Mosaic rules rather than given all at once just before Moses died.

notes.meaning: God commanded a regular daily burnt offering of two flawless, one-year-old male lambs. One lamb was sacrificed every morning and the other every evening at twilight. This regular rhythm framed each day with worship and reminded the people of their constant need for God's forgiveness and favor.

Each daily lamb was accompanied by a grain offering of fine flour mixed with the finest pressed olive oil. This daily practice was originally established at Mount Sinai and was burned on the altar to be a sweet, pleasing aroma to the Lord. Giving flour and oil alongside the animal acknowledged that daily food and earthly blessings come from God.

A drink offering of strong, choice wine was poured out near the altar for each lamb. God required the best wine to teach His people to honor Him with the finest things they possessed. The second lamb was offered at twilight in the exact same way as the morning sacrifice, closing the day in worship.

On the Sabbath day of rest, the priests presented two extra year-old lambs along with grain and drink offerings. These were offered in addition to the daily morning and evening sacrifices, not instead of them. Doubling the sacrifices showed that the Sabbath was set apart for special honor and deeper devotion to God.

At the start of each month, Israel brought a major burnt offering of two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs, all without defect. Each animal was matched with a specific amount of fine flour mixed with oil, with larger portions for the larger animals. This showed gratitude for God's care over time and dedicated the coming month to Him.

Drink offerings of wine were poured out with each monthly animal, following exact measurements. Along with these burnt offerings, the priests offered a male goat as a sin offering to ask forgiveness for any wrongs done during the past month. All these monthly sacrifices were placed on the altar on top of the regular daily offerings.

The fourteenth day of the first month was Passover, remembering how God spared His people in Egypt. The next day began the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread, when only bread made without yeast could be eaten. The first day was a sacred assembly where the people gathered for worship and did no ordinary work.

On each day of the festival, the priests offered two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs as burnt offerings. Every animal had to be completely healthy and free from flaws. Each bull and ram was paired with a generous grain offering of fine flour mixed with olive oil.

Each of the seven lambs was accompanied by its own portion of fine flour mixed with oil. In addition, one male goat was sacrificed as a sin offering to make atonement, which means restoring peace between God and His people. This taught Israel to confess their sins even while celebrating God's great deliverance.

These festival sacrifices were brought every day for seven days, right after the regular morning sacrifice. The daily burnt offering never stopped, showing that special celebrations were added to everyday worship rather than replacing it. The seventh day of the feast was another sacred assembly where all regular labor ceased.

The Feast of Weeks, also called the day of firstfruits or Pentecost, celebrated the end of the wheat harvest seven weeks after Passover. On this day, the people rested from their normal work and gathered for a holy meeting to present new grain to God. They also offered a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven year-old lambs to express their joy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the animal count here differs from Leviticus 23:18, leading to debate over whether this was an additional set of sacrifices or a differing tradition.

notes.meaning: The Feast of Weeks included specific grain offerings of flour and oil for each bull, ram, and lamb. The priests also offered one male goat as a sin offering to make atonement for the people. Even during a happy harvest celebration, this sacrifice reminded them that gratitude and confession belong together.

These harvest offerings and their drink offerings were presented in addition to the daily morning and evening sacrifices. Every animal, grain offering, wine, and oil had to be completely unblemished and of the highest quality. Giving flawless gifts taught the people that God deserves the very best of everything they have.
